I will now explore the data with Python to guide the kernel choices. ```python # Explore the time series data: summary, head, index, and a plot. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from pandas.plotting import register_matplotlib_converters register_matplotlib_converters() print("Data type:", type(data)) print("Length:", len(data)) print("Index type:", type(data.index)) print("Index freq:", data.index.freq) print("\nHead of data:") print(data.head()) print("\nDescribe:") print(data.describe()) # Plot the full series plt.figure(figsize=(12,3)) plt.plot(data.index, data.values, '-k', lw=0.8) plt.title("Time series preview") plt.xlabel("Time") plt.ylabel("Value") plt.grid(True) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() # Quick autocorrelation check (partial): compute autocorrelation for up to ~400 lags from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf lags = min(400, len(data)//2) acfs = acf(data.values, nlags=lags, fft=True) plt.figure(figsize=(10,3)) plt.stem(range(len(acfs)), acfs, use_line_collection=True) plt.title("ACF (first {} lags)".format(lags)) plt.xlabel("Lag") plt.ylabel("ACF") plt.grid(True) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() # Find an approximate dominant lag from ACF peaks (naive) peak_lags = [] for i in range(1, len(acfs)-1): if acfs[i] > acfs[i-1] and acfs[i] > acfs[i+1] and acfs[i] > 0.2: peak_lags.append(i) print("ACF candidate peak lags (lag indices with ACF > 0.2):", peak_lags[:10]) # Convert index to numeric time in days (float) to feed into GP # If index is datetime-like, convert to ordinal days if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(data.index): t = (data.index - data.index[0]).total_seconds() / (3600*24) # days since start else: # fallback: use integer index t = np.arange(len(data)) print("Time span (days):", t[-1]) # quick plot of a subset for clarity plt.figure(figsize=(12,3)) plt.plot(t, data.values, '-b', lw=0.8) plt.title("Time series vs numeric time (days since start)") plt.xlabel("Days since start") plt.ylabel("Value") plt.grid(True) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` output Reflection on exploration - The printed outputs and plots will show the observation frequency (likely daily) and the repeating on/off pattern visible in the image. The ACF should reveal a dominant lag corresponding to the period of the repeating pattern. Based on the visual reference, the series alternates between two levels (around ~10 and ~20), with a roughly monthly/seasonal periodicity—so a periodic kernel is appropriate. - A smooth kernel (Matern 3/2) will model slow trend/level drift and small lengthscale Matern or ExpQuad can capture short scale local fluctuations. - Observational noise will be included as a white-noise term. Now I propose and implement a PyMC GP model that combines: - A Matern32 kernel for medium/long-term smooth trend - A Periodic kernel (multiplicative with a small-lengthscale kernel) to capture the repeating on/off seasonal pattern - A small Matern32 (or ExpQuad) kernel for local irregularities - White noise via the gp marginal likelihood noise term I will now construct that PyMC model and find a MAP estimate. ```python # Construct and fit a PyMC GP model (MAP) with the proposed kernel composition. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Prepare X and y if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(data.index): X = ((data.index - data.index[0]).total_seconds() / (3600*24)).astype(float).reshape(-1,1) # days else: X = np.arange(len(data)).astype(float).reshape(-1,1) y = data.values print("X shape:", X.shape, "y shape:", y.shape) with pm.Model() as model: # Priors for kernel amplitudes and lengthscales sigma_trend = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_trend", sigma=5.0) ls_trend = pm.HalfNormal("ls_trend", sigma=100.0) # long lengthscale (days) trend_cov = sigma_trend**2 * pm.gp.cov.Matern32(1, ls_trend) # Periodic component (period informed by inspection / ACF) sigma_per = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_per", sigma=5.0) ls_per = pm.HalfNormal("ls_per", sigma=10.0) # controls smoothness within a period # estimate period: try to get from ACF peaks; fallback to ~30 days if unknown # We'll put a weak prior on period around 30 days with some flexibility period = pm.Normal("period", mu=30.0, sigma=10.0) periodic_cov = sigma_per**2 * pm.gp.cov.Periodic(1, ls_per, period) # Short scale local variations sigma_local = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_local", sigma=2.0) ls_local = pm.HalfNormal("ls_local", sigma=5.0) local_cov = sigma_local**2 * pm.gp.cov.Matern32(1, ls_local) # Sum of kernels: trend + periodic + local cov = trend_cov + periodic_cov + local_cov # Mean function: a linear mean can capture any linear drift intercept = pm.Normal("intercept", mu=np.mean(y), sigma=5.0) slope = pm.Normal("slope", mu=0.0, sigma=0.1) mean_func = pm.gp.mean.Linear(coeffs=slope, intercept=intercept) gp = pm.gp.Marginal(mean_func=mean_func, cov_func=cov) sigma_obs = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_obs", sigma=2.0) # observation noise y_ = gp.marginal_likelihood("y", X=X, y=y, noise=sigma_obs) # Find MAP estimate for a quick point estimate of hyperparameters map_estimate = pm.find_MAP() print("\nMAP estimate keys:", list(map_estimate.keys())) print("MAP values (some):") for k in ["sigma_trend", "ls_trend", "sigma_per", "ls_per", "period", "sigma_local", "ls_local", "sigma_obs", "intercept", "slope"]: if k in map_estimate: print(k, map_estimate[k]) ``` output Reflection on MAP fitting - The MAP search yields point estimates for the kernel hyperparameters. If the optimizer has difficulty, one can: - Reparameterize priors (e.g., log-space or tighter priors) - Use pm.sample with NUTS instead for full posterior inference (more expensive) - Initialize with sensible starting values (e.g., period near the ACF peak) - After MAP, one can compute the posterior predictive mean and credible bands using gp.conditional or gp.predict. with pm.Model() as model:
    # Trend (smooth long-term) component
    sigma_trend = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_trend", sigma=5.0)
    ls_trend = pm.HalfNormal("ls_trend", sigma=100.0)
    trend_cov = sigma_trend**2 * pm.gp.cov.Matern32(1, ls_trend)

    # Periodic component for the repeating on/off pattern
    sigma_per = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_per", sigma=5.0)
    ls_per = pm.HalfNormal("ls_per", sigma=10.0)
    period = pm.Normal("period", mu=30.0, sigma=10.0)  # weak prior; MAP will adjust
    periodic_cov = sigma_per**2 * pm.gp.cov.Periodic(1, ls_per, period)

    # Local short-scale variations
    sigma_local = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_local", sigma=2.0)
    ls_local = pm.HalfNormal("ls_local", sigma=5.0)
    local_cov = sigma_local**2 * pm.gp.cov.Matern32(1, ls_local)

    # Sum the kernels
    cov = trend_cov + periodic_cov + local_cov

    # Linear mean to capture overall level + trend
    intercept = pm.Normal("intercept", mu=np.mean(y), sigma=5.0)
    slope = pm.Normal("slope", mu=0.0, sigma=0.1)
    mean_func = pm.gp.mean.Linear(coeffs=slope, intercept=intercept)

    # GP marginal model
    gp = pm.gp.Marginal(mean_func=mean_func, cov_func=cov)

    # Observation noise (use sigma= in marginal_likelihood)
    sigma_obs = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_obs", sigma=2.0)
    y_ = gp.marginal_likelihood("y", X=X, y=y, sigma=sigma_obs)

    # Find MAP (point estimate of hyperparameters)
    map_estimate = pm.find_MAP()
